about.title: Volume of Cones and Spheres
about.length_note: About 35 minutes. There are four topics: the cone, the sphere, mixed solids, and exact versus rounded answers. Each one gets a worked example and a check question. You can pause after any question and carry on later.

say.text: Welcome! Last class you found the volume of cylinders. Today we add two more solids: the cone and the sphere.

show.text: Volume of Cones and Spheres

say.text: First, a quick reminder. A cylinder's volume is pi times the radius squared times the height.

show.text: Cylinder: V = πr²h

ask.q: A cylinder has radius 3 and height 5. What is its volume, leaving π as a symbol?
ask.why: Square the radius first: 3 × 3 = 9. Then multiply by the height: 9 × 5 = 45, so the volume is 45π. 15π means the radius was never squared. 30π comes from 2 × 3 × 5, which is doubling instead of squaring. 225π comes from squaring 3 × 5 instead of just the radius.

say.text: Now the cone. A cone has a flat round base that narrows to a point at the other end.

show.text: A cone, like an ice-cream cone or a party hat: a flat circle at the bottom, narrowing up to one point.

say.text: Picture a cone standing inside a cylinder. They have the same base and the same height. The cone fills only part of the cylinder.

show.text: A glass cylinder with a cone sitting inside it. Both have the same circle on the bottom and reach the same height.

say.text: How much of it? Try pouring. Fill the cone with water and pour it into the cylinder. It takes exactly three cones to fill it.

show.text: Three cone-fulls fill one cylinder

say.text: So a cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

ask.q: A cylinder holds 60 cm³. A cone has the same base and the same height. How much does the cone hold?
ask.why: The cone is one third of the cylinder, so divide by 3: 60 ÷ 3 = 20. 180 comes from multiplying by 3, which would be a bigger solid than the cylinder. 30 is half, not a third. 57 comes from subtracting 3.

say.text: Since the cone is one third of the cylinder, its formula is the cylinder formula times one third. Here r is the radius and h is the height.

show.text: Cone: V = ⅓πr²h

say.text: Example: a cone with radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. The base part is π × 16. Times 10 gives 160π. One third of that is 160π/3, about 167.55 cm³.
Your turn. For now, leave π as a symbol and give your answer as a number times π.

show.text: V = ⅓πr²h

ask.q: A cone has radius 3 and height 7. What is its volume?
ask.why: Square the radius: 3 × 3 = 9. Multiply by the height: 9 × 7 = 63. Take one third: 63 ÷ 3 = 21, so 21π. 63π forgets the one third. 7π forgets to square the radius. 147π squares 3 × 7 by mistake and then takes a third.

say.text: Watch out for diameter. The formulas need the radius, which is half the diameter. A cone has diameter 12 cm and height 14 cm. So r = 6, and the volume is ⅓ × π × 36 × 14 = 168π cm³.

show.text: diameter 12, so radius 6 | 6² = 36 | ⅓ × 36 × 14 = 168 | V = 168π cm³

ask.q: A cone has diameter 10 and height 9. What is its volume?
ask.why: Halve the diameter to get the radius: 5. Then ⅓ × 25 × 9 = 75, so 75π. 300π uses 10 as the radius. 225π forgets the one third. 15π forgets to square the radius.

say.text: On to the sphere. A sphere is a perfectly round solid, like a ball. It has no height to measure. The only measurement is the radius.

show.text: A ball with a line from its centre to its surface, labelled r for radius.

say.text: The sphere formula is four thirds times pi times the radius cubed. Cubed means r × r × r, not r squared.

show.text: Sphere: V = ⁴⁄₃πr³

say.text: Example: a sphere with radius 3 m. First 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Then ⁴⁄₃ of 27 is 36. So the volume is 36π, about 113.10 m³.

ask.q: A sphere has radius 6. What is its volume?
ask.why: Cube the radius: 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. Then ⁴⁄₃ × 216 = 288, so 288π. 48π squares the radius instead of cubing it. 864π multiplies by 4 but forgets to divide by 3. 24π multiplies the radius by 3 instead of cubing it.

say.text: Where does the four thirds come from? Fit a sphere snugly inside a cylinder. The cylinder's height is then 2r. The sphere fills exactly two thirds of it.

show.text: A ball fitting perfectly inside a cylinder. It touches the sides, the top and the bottom. The cylinder's height is 2r.

ask.q: A sphere fits snugly inside a cylinder that holds 90 cm³. How much does the sphere hold?
ask.why: The sphere is two thirds of the cylinder: 90 ÷ 3 = 30, then 30 × 2 = 60. 30 is only one third. 45 is half. 120 is bigger than the cylinder, which can't be right because the sphere sits inside it.

say.text: A Greek mathematician named Archimedes worked this out over two thousand years ago. He was so proud of it that a sphere and cylinder were put on his tomb.

show.text: A sphere inside a cylinder, the picture Archimedes asked to have on his tomb.

say.text: Here is a neat link. Take a cone and a sphere with the same radius, where the height is 2r. Put their volumes together and you get the cylinder. So the sphere holds two cones' worth.

show.text: cone + sphere = cylinder (when h = 2r)

ask.q: A cone, a sphere and a cylinder share the same radius, and the height is 2r. The cone holds 12 mL. How much does the sphere hold?
ask.why: The sphere holds as much as two cones: 2 × 12 = 24. 36 mL is the whole cylinder, which is three cones. 4 mL divides by 3 instead of multiplying by 2. 16 mL multiplies by ⁴⁄₃, which mixes up the formulas.

say.text: Let's see it as bars. The radius is 3 and the height is 6. In units of π, the cone is 18, the sphere is 36 and the cylinder is 54.

show.text: Same radius 3, height 6

say.text: Now mixed solids. A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is half of ⁴⁄₃. That makes it ⅔πr³.

show.text: Hemisphere: V = ⅔πr³

ask.q: A hemisphere has radius 6. What is its volume?
ask.why: ⅔ × 216 = 144, so 144π. 288π is the whole sphere. 24π squares the radius instead of cubing it. 432π multiplies by 2 but forgets to divide by 3.

say.text: Mixed problem: an ice-cream cone with a half-ball of ice cream on top. Both have radius 3 cm, and the cone is 8 cm tall. Split it into two solids and add.

show.text: Cone: ⅓ × π × 9 × 8 = 24π | Hemisphere: ⅔ × π × 27 = 18π | Total: 24π + 18π = 42π cm³

say.text: Same idea for a toy: a cylinder with a cone on top, both with radius 2. The cylinder is 5 tall. The cone is 3 tall.

show.text: A toy made of a cylinder with a pointed cone sitting on its top circle. Both have radius 2.

ask.q: The cylinder has radius 2 and height 5. The cone on top has radius 2 and height 3. What is the total volume?
ask.why: Cylinder: 4 × 5 = 20, so 20π. Cone: ⅓ × 4 × 3 = 4, so 4π. Add them: 24π. 32π forgets the one third on the cone. 16π subtracts instead of adding. 20π leaves the cone out.

say.text: Last topic: how to write the answer. Leaving π as a symbol, like 288π, is exact. Rounding means using a number for π. That gives an approximate answer, and you write cubic units.

show.text: Sphere, radius 6 | Exact: 288π | With π ≈ 3.14: 904.32 | With a calculator's π: about 904.78

ask.q: Which of these is the exact volume of a sphere with radius 6?
ask.why: Only 288π keeps π as a symbol, so nothing has been rounded. 904.32 and 904.78 are approximations. 288 on its own has lost the π, so it is a different number.

say.text: When a question says use 3.14, do exactly that. Your answer may differ slightly from a calculator's answer, and that's fine.

show.text: Follow the question: π ≈ 3.14, or in terms of π

ask.q: Use π ≈ 3.14. A cone has radius 3 and height 7, so its volume is 21π. What is the volume as a decimal?
ask.why: 21 × 3.14 = 65.94. 197.82 is 63 × 3.14, which forgets the one third. 65.97 uses a calculator's π, but the question said to use 3.14. 21.98 is 7 × 3.14, which forgets to square the radius.

say.text: Let's gather it up. The cylinder is πr²h. The cone is a third of that. The sphere is ⁴⁄₃πr³, and the hemisphere is half of the sphere. Always use the radius.

show.text: Cylinder: πr²h | Cone: ⅓πr²h | Sphere: ⁴⁄₃πr³ | Hemisphere: ⅔πr³ | Same base and height: cone = ⅓ cylinder

ask.q: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height. The cone's volume is 8π. What is the cylinder's volume?
ask.why: The cone is one third of the cylinder, so the cylinder is three times the cone: 3 × 8π = 24π. 8π/3 divides when you should multiply. 16π would be only twice the cone. 11π adds 3 instead of multiplying by 3.

notes.topic: Leaving answers in terms of pi

other_side.claim: Pouring water shows that a cone is one third of a cylinder.
other_side.other_view: Pouring is a good demonstration, but it is measuring, not proof. A full proof needs more advanced tools. One source says the usual proof uses calculus. Archimedes got there by comparing slices of the shapes.

other_side.claim: You should round π to 3.14 when you need a decimal answer.
other_side.other_view: Teachers and worksheets differ. Some use 3.14 and some use a calculator's π. Some prefer exact answers like 288π. The same sphere comes out as 904.32 with 3.14 and about 904.78 with a calculator. Follow what each question asks for.
